title: Pipes: The Power of Connection 🔗
description: Understand pipes from the inside – how they connect processes, their exit statuses, and subshell behaviour.

slides.title: The Magic of `|` ✨
slides.content:
## Stdout ➡️ Stdin

A **pipe** (`|`) connects the standard output of one command to the standard input of the next. It's the backbone of Unix philosophy: small, composable tools.

```bash
command1 | command2 | command3
```
Data flows from left to right, processed in stages.

slides.title: Simple Pipe
slides.content: Count how many shell users exist:

quizData.question: What does `ls -l | wc -l` do?

options.text: Counts the number of files and directories
Lists long format and then word count

quizData.explanation: `ls -l` output is piped to `wc -l`, which counts lines.

slides.title: Pipes Create Subshells 👯
slides.content:
## Each command in a pipeline runs in a subshell.

This means variables changed inside the pipeline are lost afterward.

```bash
a=5
echo "hi" | { a=10; echo "$a"; }  # prints 10 inside
echo "$a"  # still 5
```
To capture modifications, use process substitution or redirect the final output.

slides.title: Variable Scope in Pipelines
slides.content: Try to modify a variable in a pipeline:
slides.codeSnippet:
total=0
find . -type f | while read f; do
  ((total++))
done
echo "Total files: $total"  # 0!

quizData.question: A variable changed inside a `while` loop that is part of a pipeline will be visible after the pipeline.
quizData.explanation: Because the loop runs in a subshell, its variable changes are lost when the pipeline ends.

slides.title: Exit Status of Pipelines 🚦
slides.content:
## Which Command's Exit Code Wins?

By default, the exit status of a pipeline is the exit status of the **last** command.

```bash
false | true
echo $?  # 0
```
To get the status of any command, use the `PIPESTATUS` array (Bash‑only). It holds the exit codes of all parts in the last pipeline.

slides.title: Fail Fast with `set -o pipefail` 🛑
slides.content:
## Stop on Any Failure

If you want the pipeline to fail if **any** command fails, enable pipefail:

```bash
set -o pipefail
false | true
echo $?  # 1
```
This is essential for robust scripts.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Use `trap` to handle errors and `set -e` together with `pipefail` for strict error checking in production scripts.
